readings.title: The Story of Mankind: up the tower of Saint Lawrence (Foreword, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a climb floor by floor and notice how each level changes what the boy hears and sees.
readings.focus: Van Loon opens a history book with a childhood memory, building a comparison he explains only at the end.
readings.context: Hendrik Willem van Loon grew up in the Netherlands and wrote The Story of Mankind in New York for his sons Hansje and Willem; in 1922 it won the first Newbery Medal for American children’s literature. Saint Lawrence is the great medieval church of Rotterdam. A sexton looks after a church building; an apothecary is an old word for a chemist or pharmacist.

excerpt.locator: Foreword, from “For Hansje and Willem” through the boy’s first view from the highest gallery; opens “For Hansje and Willem:”; closes “It was my first glimpse of the big world.”.

questions.prompt: List the floors of the tower in order. What does the boy find on each one?
facilitatorNotes: Dark stairs; a storeroom of old carved images under dust; a room of pigeons and barred windows; the town clock; the bells; the highest gallery. Each level brings a new sense: silence, darkness, light, music, rhythm, sound and at last the whole view.
evidence: We went to the next floor and then to the next and the next until I had lost count
We had reached the highest gallery.

questions.prompt: What could “audible silence” and “tangible darkness” mean? Why put such opposite-seeming words together?
facilitatorNotes: Silence so complete that you seem to hear it, darkness so thick that you seem to touch it. The paradoxes show a boy meeting experiences for which ordinary words do not work.
evidence: the phenomenon of audible silence
that of tangible darkness

questions.prompt: How does the noise of the town change when it is heard from high up? Which words show the change?
facilitatorNotes: Carts, hoofs, cranes and steam are “purified and cleansed by the distance” into “a softly rustling whisper.” Distance turns noise into music, which prepares for the Foreword’s later claim that a height, and history, can turn confusion into order.
evidence: purified and cleansed by the distance
a softly rustling whisper

questions.prompt: In the storeroom, carved saints lie in dust among rats and spiders. What does van Loon want us to notice about things that once “meant life and death”?
facilitatorNotes: Objects at the centre of people’s faith became junk when beliefs changed (Rotterdam’s church became Protestant in the sixteenth century, and its Catholic images were put away). Readers may find the scene sad, funny (“opened up shop”) or both; either way the past is stored, forgotten and waiting to be found.
evidence: That which had meant life and death to our ancestors was here reduced to junk and rubbish.

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the watchman’s view and the Tower of Experience (Foreword, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison from a real tower to an idea, and explain what each part of it stands for.
readings.focus: The Foreword turns a remembered view into an argument for why history is worth the climb.
readings.context: Recap: as a boy, van Loon climbed with his uncle to the top gallery of the Saint Lawrence tower in Rotterdam and saw the city from above for the first time. The watchman points to Dutch places and people: William the Silent, Prince of Orange, who led the Dutch revolt against Spain in the 1500s; the admirals De Ruyter and Tromp; Grotius, a scholar of law; and Erasmus, a famous writer. Leyden, Delft and Gouda are Dutch towns.

excerpt.locator: Foreword, from “Since then, whenever I have had the opportunity” to the signature; opens “Since then, whenever I have had the opportunity, I have gone to the top of the tower and…”; closes “HENDRIK WILLEM VAN LOON.”.

questions.prompt: What did the watchman know, and how had he learned it?
facilitatorNotes: He had little schooling and rarely read a book, but living on the tower he had “absorbed the wisdom” of the land around him, so history was “a living thing” he could point to. Readers may discuss whether learning by place counts as knowing history.
evidence: he had rarely read a book
History he knew well, for it was a living thing with him.

questions.prompt: Choose one place the watchman points to. What happened there, and how does seeing the place change the story?
facilitatorNotes: The bend of the river where the dikes were cut to save Leyden; Delft, where William the Silent was murdered; Gouda, Erasmus’s early home. The landscape becomes a map of events, and the river turns from a harbour into “a wonderful highroad.”
evidence: That is where the Prince of Orange cut the dikes to drown the land and save Leyden.
became a wonderful highroad

questions.prompt: Complete the comparison: if history is the tower, what are the climb, the view and the key?
facilitatorNotes: The climb is the hard work of learning (“no easy task”); the view is understanding how the present came to be; the key is this book. “Young feet are strong” tells young readers he expects them to manage it.
evidence: History is the mighty Tower of Experience
Here I give you the key that will open the door.

questions.prompt: How does the view change the way the boy sees his ordinary home? Do you think knowing history can do the same?
facilitatorNotes: Confused commotion becomes “the well-ordered expression of human energy and purpose,” and the past gives “new courage.” Readers may agree, or argue that history can also be discouraging; ask for a reason either way.
evidence: But the tower showed us the old home in a new light.
gave us new courage to face the problems of the future

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: a question mark and the first living things (Chapter 1, first part)
readings.challenge: Tell apart what the writer says is known, what he says is guessed, and what is a storyteller’s way of putting things.
readings.focus: A history of mankind begins with unimaginable time and with the writer’s admission of how little anyone knows.
readings.context: Recap: the Foreword compared history to a tower that gives a wide view. The book itself opens with a legend about eternity (Svithjod is an old name for Sweden). The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; the notes point out the main changes. Where van Loon writes “a line of this length,” his book shows a long line beside a tiny one; the drawing is not reproduced here.

excerpt.locator: Opening epigraph and “The Setting of the Stage,” from its start through the first amphibians; opens “High up in the North in the land called Svithjod, there stands a rock. It is a hundred…”; closes “…your path can tell you all about the pleasures of the double existence of the amphibian.”.

questions.prompt: What does the legend of the rock and the little bird ask you to imagine? Why might a history book begin with it?
facilitatorNotes: A rock a hundred miles high, worn away by one bird’s visits every thousand years, to make a single day of eternity: time beyond imagining. It prepares readers for the millions of years in the chapter and makes human history look very short.
evidence: Once every thousand years a little bird comes to this rock to sharpen its beak.
then a single day of eternity will have gone by.

questions.prompt: Find words in which van Loon admits that he is not certain. Why does he need so many in this chapter?
facilitatorNotes: “We still know very little,” “with a fair degree of accuracy,” “according to our best belief,” “as far as we now know.” No one saw the beginning of life; it is reconstructed from evidence. Ask which later sentences carry no such warning.
evidence: We still know very little
according to our best belief
as far as we now know

questions.prompt: Van Loon says plants “reluctantly” left the water and “after centuries of training” learned to live in the air. Is that how it really happened? Why might he write it this way?
facilitatorNotes: Plants did not choose or train. Over very many generations, those suited to new places survived and spread. The wording turns a slow process into a story with characters. Readers can rewrite one sentence without the choosing words and compare the two.
evidence: Reluctantly they left the water
After centuries of training

questions.prompt: Why, according to van Loon, does the book study human beings rather than cats or horses? Is it a fair reason?
facilitatorNotes: Humans were “the first to use his brain for the purpose of conquering the forces of nature.” Some readers accept that people make history in a way animals do not; others point out that he himself grants animals “a very interesting historical development.”
evidence: Man was the last to come but the first to use his brain
have a very interesting historical development behind them

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: giant reptiles, birds and mammals (Chapter 1, end)
readings.challenge: Compare the writer’s confident explanations with what he admits he does not know, and notice where he speaks directly to the reader.
readings.focus: Van Loon makes a huge stretch of time feel familiar through cats, kittens and a child learning to walk.
readings.context: Recap: van Loon has followed life from the first cell in the sea to plants and amphibians on land. Since he wrote, scientists have found that birds descend from small feathered dinosaurs and that a giant asteroid helped end the age of the great reptiles; human beings are not descended from today’s apes or monkeys but share distant ancestors with them.

excerpt.locator: “The Setting of the Stage,” from “Once outside of the water” to the end of the chapter; opens “Once outside of the water, these animals gradually adapted themselves more and more to…”; closes “This creature, though you may hardly believe it, was your first “man-like” ancestor.”.

questions.prompt: What does van Loon say about why the giant reptiles died? How certain is he?
facilitatorNotes: “We do not know the reason,” followed by two “Perhaps” guesses: a change in climate, or growing too big to move. His caution was right in 1921; scientists now point to an asteroid impact.
evidence: We do not know the reason.
Perhaps it was due to a sudden change in climate.

questions.prompt: How does van Loon explain the way birds came to be? Which parts sound like a guess told as a fact?
facilitatorNotes: Tree-living reptiles turned skin into a “parachute,” covered it with feathers and made their tails into “steering gear.” No “perhaps” appears, though the evidence was thin; scientists now trace birds to small feathered dinosaurs. A useful habit: notice confident sentences about things no one could watch.
evidence: they changed a part of their skin into a sort of parachute
developed into true birds

questions.prompt: What gave mammals an advantage, according to the chapter? Which everyday example does van Loon use?
facilitatorNotes: They kept and sheltered their young, who learned from their mothers, as a cat teaches her kittens to wash and catch mice. A familiar sight explains something no one saw.
evidence: the mammals kept their young with them for a long time
a cat teaching her kittens

questions.prompt: Find two places where van Loon speaks to “you.” What effect does that have?
facilitatorNotes: “You know them well,” “your less familiar cousins behind the bars of the zoological garden,” “though you may hardly believe it.” He makes the reader part of the story, and he expects surprise at the last sentence.
evidence: your less familiar cousins behind the bars of the zoological garden
This creature, though you may hardly believe it, was your first “man-like” ancestor.

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: our earliest ancestors (Chapter 2)
readings.challenge: Weigh a vivid description against the writer’s own admission of how little is known.
readings.focus: A chapter that paints early life in detail ends by saying that “the rest is darkness.”
readings.context: Recap: Chapter 1 ended with a “man-like” creature that could stand on its hind legs and was beginning to turn grunts into speech. Anthropologists study human beings, including ancient bones. Many more fossils have been found since 1921, and scientists now think the first humans arose in Africa.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon writes that the first people lived in forests “as the pygmies of Africa do to this very day,” a comparison that treats a living people as if they belonged to the distant past. It reflects a prejudice common in his time and is wrong.

excerpt.locator: “Our Earliest Ancestors,” the whole chapter; opens “We know very little about the first “true” men. We have never seen their pictures. In the…”; closes “It is little enough we know and the rest is darkness.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence of the first “true” men does van Loon say scientists have?
facilitatorNotes: Pieces of bone from the deepest layers of soil, among skeletons of extinct animals: “a few collar-bones and a few pieces of his skull.” No pictures, tools or houses. The chapter’s last line admits how little that is.
evidence: In the deepest layer of clay of an ancient soil we have sometimes found pieces of their bones.
It is little enough we know and the rest is darkness.

questions.prompt: Choose three details of early man’s daily life from the chapter. Could bones alone tell us those things?
facilitatorNotes: Hiding his family in hollow trees, catching a sparrow or a rabbit, liking to “jabber.” Bones might show size or the shape of a jaw, but not habits or feelings; much is imagined so that readers can picture the past. Sort details into “could be shown by evidence” and “imagined.”
evidence: he hid his wife and his children in a hollow tree
he endlessly repeated the same unintelligible gibberish

questions.prompt: How does van Loon think language began? Which word tells you it is a guess?
facilitatorNotes: Warning shrieks came to mean “there is a tiger!” and others grunted back. “Probably” marks it as a guess, and a reasonable one.
evidence: And this was probably the origin of all language.

questions.prompt: The chapter calls this ancestor “very ugly and unattractive” and compares him with “the pygmies of Africa.” What do these judgments tell us about the writer and his time rather than about early humans?
facilitatorNotes: “Ugly” is an opinion, not evidence. The pygmy comparison wrongly treats living people as left over from the past, a prejudice common in 1921 that scientists and historians reject. Practise separating a writer’s judgments from his evidence.
evidence: a very ugly and unattractive mammal
as the pygmies of Africa do to this very day

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: ice, fire and the first tools (Chapter 3)
readings.challenge: Notice where history is told as a story with invented moments, and ask what each story is meant to explain.
readings.focus: Van Loon argues that hardship made people inventive: the ice became mankind’s “greatest teacher.”
readings.context: Recap: van Loon has described the earliest people as wanderers who left little behind but bones. This chapter turns to the Ice Ages, when glaciers covered much of northern Europe. “Hibernal” means wintry. Scientists now count many advances of the ice rather than four, and think people used fire long before the last Ice Age.
readings.contentNote: Starving strangers are driven off in a battle in which whole families are killed; people die in blizzards and under a glacier.

excerpt.locator: “Prehistoric Man,” the whole chapter; opens “Early man did not know what time meant. He kept no records of birthdays or wedding…”; closes “…the human race, became its greatest teacher because it forced man to use his brain.”.

questions.prompt: What signs told the people of the forest that something was wrong?
facilitatorNotes: Summer came late, fruit did not ripen, snow buried the grassy mountaintops, starving strangers came down from the peaks, and the days shortened too soon. The warnings build before the glacier arrives.
evidence: Something was the matter with the weather.
The fruits had not ripened.

questions.prompt: List the problems the cold created and how people solved each one.
facilitatorNotes: Clothing: pit traps, and the skins of bears and hyenas. Housing: caves taken from animals. Cold: fire. Winter food: stores kept in clay jars. Each solution answers a problem, which is how van Loon organizes the chapter.
evidence: In the first place it was necessary that man clothe himself lest he freeze to death.
Next came the housing problem.

questions.prompt: “One evening a dead chicken fell into the fire.” Could anyone know that? Why might van Loon include it?
facilitatorNotes: No one could; it is an invented scene showing how cooking might have been discovered, turning a slow change into one memorable moment. Discuss whether invented scenes help or mislead in a history book, and how a reader can tell them from evidence.
evidence: And then one evening a dead chicken fell into the fire.

questions.prompt: How can a terrible danger become a “teacher”? Do you agree with van Loon’s conclusion?
facilitatorNotes: Hardship forced people to think, invent tools and plan ahead. Some readers agree; others note that luck, cooperation and place also mattered, and that the same hardship killed many. Ask for reasons drawn from the chapter.
evidence: Only the people with the cleverest brains survived.
became its greatest teacher because it forced man to use his brain

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the Rosetta Stone (Chapter 4, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a story of discovery step by step, separating the clue, the plan and the result.
readings.focus: Writing preserves experience, and one stone with three inscriptions made a lost script readable again.
readings.context: Recap: van Loon left the early Europeans in their caves, learning to use fire and tools, and now turns to Egypt. Bonaparte is Napoleon, the French general who later became emperor; papyrus is a writing material made from reeds. Some of van Loon’s details are wrong: hieroglyphs were still carved for some four hundred years after the Romans came, and Champollion, a boy of eleven in 1802, announced his breakthrough in 1822.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon calls the early Europeans “savages” and generalizes about “Indian” picture messages in adventure stories of the American West.

excerpt.locator: “Hieroglyphics,” from the chapter’s opening through Champollion’s discovery of phonetic writing; opens “These earliest ancestors of ours who lived in the great European wilderness were rapidly…”; closes “…words into a written form, with the help of only a few dots and dashes and pothooks.”.

questions.prompt: Why does van Loon call writing “the most important of all inventions”? What comparison does he use?
facilitatorNotes: Without writing we would be like cats and dogs, who teach their young a few things but cannot use the experience of earlier generations. Readers may weigh other candidates, such as fire or the wheel.
evidence: writing, the most important of all inventions, is quite new
possess no way in which they can make use of the experience of those generations

questions.prompt: What made the Rosetta stone different from every other carved stone in Egypt?
facilitatorNotes: It carried three inscriptions, one of them in Greek, which scholars could read. If all three said the same thing, the known Greek could unlock the unknown Egyptian.
evidence: It carried three inscriptions. One of these was in Greek.
is to compare the Greek text with the Egyptian figures

questions.prompt: The officer thought the task would be simple. What happened instead?
facilitatorNotes: It took more than twenty years. The distance between the confident plan (“at once”) and the result shows how hard decipherment is.
evidence: The plan sounded simple enough but it took more than twenty years to solve the riddle.

questions.prompt: Explain the riddle of the man with the saw in your own words. What did Champollion discover?
facilitatorNotes: A picture cannot always mean the thing it shows: a queen of eighty-two does not use a saw. So some pictures must stand for sounds, and Egyptian writing used signs for sounds as well as for things. Readers can invent a picture-pun of their own, such as an eye for “I.”
evidence: Queens of eighty-two do not handle saws.
a system of characters which reproduce the “sound” (or phone) of the spoken word

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the Nile, the dead and the pyramids (Chapter 5)
readings.challenge: Trace a chain of causes from a river’s flood to a five-hundred-foot tomb.
readings.focus: Plentiful food gave the Egyptians leisure, leisure gave them questions, and the answers made a “land devoted to the Dead.”
readings.context: Van Loon has told how the Egyptian script was deciphered; the rest of that chapter, which shows a sentence in hieroglyphs with drawings that cannot be printed here, is skipped. Osiris and Isis were Egyptian gods; natron is a natural salt used to dry bodies. Some details are out of date: archaeologists now think the Great Pyramid’s builders numbered perhaps twenty to thirty thousand, and “pyramid” comes from a Greek word, not an Egyptian one.

excerpt.locator: “The Nile Valley,” the whole chapter; opens “The history of man is the record of a hungry creature in search of food. Wherever food…”; closes “…by the weight of those thousands of tons of stone which press upon it from all sides.”.

questions.prompt: How did the Nile “do the work of a million men”?
facilitatorNotes: Each summer its flood covered the fields with fertile clay, and canals and well-sweeps carried the water further. Farmers needed less labour, so large cities could be fed.
evidence: In Egypt a kindly river did the work of a million men
covered with several inches of the most fertile clay

questions.prompt: What did the Egyptians do with the leisure that easy farming gave them?
facilitatorNotes: They made ornaments that were “not the least bit useful” and asked large questions: where the stars come from, who makes the thunder, why the Nile rises, who they themselves are. Leisure leads to art, science and religion.
evidence: He used this spare time to make himself many things that were merely ornamental
Where did the stars come from?

questions.prompt: Follow the steps from graves cut in rock to the Great Pyramid. What caused each change?
facilitatorNotes: Moving north meant burying in the desert; animals and robbers broke in; mounds of stones protected the graves; the rich competed to build higher; King Khufu built the highest. Readers may question whether rivalry alone explains the pyramids.
evidence: there was a good deal of competition to see who could make the highest hill of stones
The record was made by King Khufu

questions.prompt: Where does van Loon admit that he does not understand something? How does that affect your trust in the rest?
facilitatorNotes: Of ferrying the stones across the Nile he says “we do not understand.” An honest admission can make a writer more believable, though readers should still check his confident claims, such as the number of workers.
evidence: how they ever managed to do this, we do not understand

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: Egypt’s conquerors and the land between the rivers (Chapters 6 and 7)
readings.challenge: Keep a long line of rulers and invaders in order, and notice which events van Loon slows down to tell as a story.
readings.focus: Egypt’s three thousand years end in a chain of conquests, while a second river valley rises; van Loon explains both by their rivers.
readings.context: Van Loon has explained how the Nile’s yearly flood fed Egypt and how its kings built the pyramids; now he races through Egypt’s history and then turns east. Pharaoh is the title of the Egyptian kings; Osiris was the Egyptian god of the dead; Thebes was the great city of southern Egypt; Sardanapalus is the Greek name for an Assyrian king; the Ptolemies were the Greek-speaking family that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great. In the Bible, Noah’s Ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat, in the region of Armenia. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; historians now think the Hyksos came from Canaan and other lands of western Asia, not Arabia, and ruled northern Egypt for about a century, until about 1550 B.C.; Cleopatra, herself one of the Ptolemies, died in 30 B.C., and Augustus was Caesar’s great-nephew and adopted son.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon calls the Hyksos “a savage Arab tribe” and says the Hebrews in Egypt were hated for serving them as tax-gatherers, a claim no ancient record supports. He puts Cleopatra’s power down to her “beauty and charm,” an old habit of belittling women rulers, and says endless war made the people of Mesopotamia “a very strong race,” a racial idea historians reject. Cleopatra’s death by poison is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of Egypt” and “Mesopotamia,” both whole chapters; opens “The river Nile was a kind friend but occasionally it was a hard taskmaster. It taught the…”; closes “…of creating a civilisation which was in every respect as important as that of Egypt.”.

questions.prompt: According to van Loon, how did the Nile turn neighbours into a state, and the state into a kingdom? Name the steps.
facilitatorNotes: The river forced “team-work”: people had to build and repair trenches and dikes together, so their “mutual-benefit-association” became an organised state. When neighbours from Asia invaded, one strong man led the defence and became King. A river shapes a government; readers can ask whether danger from outside is the usual way leaders gain power.
evidence: It taught the people who lived along its banks the noble art of “team-work.”
he became the leader of the community and their commander-in-chief

questions.prompt: What did the peasant of the grain fields care about, and what did he not care about? What does that suggest about whose history usually gets told?
facilitatorNotes: He cared little for the Pharaohs’ “political adventures” as long as taxes seemed fair, but hated foreign invaders who robbed him. Most Egyptians were such peasants, yet the chapter is a list of kings and conquerors. Readers can imagine what a peasant’s history of Egypt would put in and leave out.
evidence: rarely interested the patient and toiling peasant of the grain fields
Provided he was not obliged to pay more taxes to his King than he thought just

questions.prompt: Cleopatra is the only ruler van Loon describes at any length. What does he say made her dangerous? Is that a fair way to describe a queen who governed a country?
facilitatorNotes: He says her “beauty and charm” were worth more than “half a dozen Egyptian army corps.” That reduces a ruler to her looks; she ran a state, led fleets and dealt with Rome for twenty years. He also grants that she “tried her best to save the country,” so readers may find a little respect alongside the old cliché.
evidence: Her beauty and charm were more dangerous to the Roman generals than half a dozen Egyptian army corps.
tried her best to save the country

questions.prompt: Van Loon gives Egypt and Mesopotamia the same attraction. What is it, and what different result does he say it had between the two rivers? Does constant war really make a people “strong”?
facilitatorNotes: Both offered “food upon fairly easy terms.” But Mesopotamia lay open to mountain people and desert nomads, so their rivalry brought “endless warfare,” and he concludes that only “the strongest and the bravest” survived. That is a guess, not evidence: war also destroys towns, harvests and learning, and the valley’s peoples mixed rather than forming one race. His hawk’s-eye view from the pyramid is a storyteller’s bridge between two places a thousand miles apart.
evidence: offered them food upon fairly easy terms
Only the strongest and the bravest could hope to survive
imagine yourself possessed of the eyes of a hawk

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the nail writers of Mesopotamia (Chapter 8)
readings.challenge: Follow a story of decipherment across four centuries, then keep a long chain of conquering peoples in order.
readings.focus: Wedge-shaped writing on clay kept the history of a valley that one people after another conquered and that ended as mounds of earth.
readings.context: Van Loon has told how Champollion learned to read Egyptian hieroglyphs. Cuneiform, the “nail-writing” of this chapter, was pressed into wet clay with a pointed reed. Van Loon’s book shows small drawings of the signs; they are not reproduced here, so a few sentences in the fourth paragraph have gaps where a drawing stood. Kathay is an old name for China; Shiraz is a city in Iran; the inscription of Behistun is carved high on a cliff in Iran and, like the Rosetta stone, gives one text in three languages. The Sumerians’ “towers” are the stepped temple-mounds called ziggurats. Exile is being forced to live far from home; tribute is payment demanded by a conqueror. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; no one knows where the Sumerians came from, and their dates are uncertain.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon calls the Sumerians “a white people” and groups other peoples as “Semites,” a name he explains came from an old belief that they descended from Noah’s son Shem. Today “Semitic” names a family of languages, including Akkadian, Hebrew and Arabic, not a race. The chapter tells of centuries of conquest, destruction and exile.

excerpt.locator: “The Sumerians,” the whole chapter; opens “The fifteenth century was an age of great discoveries. Columbus tried to find a way to…”; closes “…became a vast wilderness where huge mounds of earth told a story of ancient glory.”.

questions.prompt: Why does van Loon say the nail-writing was harder to read than Egyptian hieroglyphs?
facilitatorNotes: The Egyptians kept pictures, but the Sumerians “discarded pictures entirely” for V-shaped marks that hardly resembled what they stood for; a star even came to mean “heaven.” So there was no picture to guess from. Readers can draw a star and simplify it into a few wedge strokes to see how fast the picture disappears.
evidence: the job of Champollion had been an easy one
had discarded pictures entirely

questions.prompt: Put the people who helped to read cuneiform in order. What did each one add, and how long did the whole effort take?
facilitatorNotes: Barbero reported strange carvings in the fifteenth century; Niebuhr brought inscriptions to Europe at the end of the eighteenth; thirty years later Grotefend read four letters, the name Darius; twenty years after that Rawlinson’s Behistun inscription gave “a workable key.” Several centuries and several countries: each person built on the last, as in a relay.
evidence: a patient German school-master by the name of Grotefend
gave us a workable key to the nail-writing of western Asia

questions.prompt: Van Loon says modern engineers borrowed an idea from the Sumerians. What idea, and how good is his evidence?
facilitatorNotes: The sloping galleries around their towers, like the ramps in big railroad stations. It is a likeness, not proof: engineers could have invented ramps without knowing about Sumer. The very next sentence, “we do not know it,” admits how little can be traced. Readers can think of other inventions that people in different places made separately.
evidence: Our engineers have borrowed this idea
We may have borrowed other ideas from the Sumerians but we do not know it.

questions.prompt: The last paragraph names one conquering people after another. Find two who built something and two who destroyed. Why does van Loon call the valley a “melting-pot,” and how does the chapter end?
facilitatorNotes: Builders: Hammurabi, who gave laws, and the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar, whose astronomy and mathematics van Loon praises. Destroyers: the Hittites, who “destroyed whatever they could not carry away,” and the Assyrians’ “vast and terrible empire.” A melting-pot mixes many peoples into one place, a phrase Americans of 1921 used about immigration to the United States. The ending, mounds of earth where cities stood, shows how completely even great empires can vanish.
evidence: gave his people a set of laws
destroyed whatever they could not carry away
the old melting-pot of so many Semitic races
huge mounds of earth told a story of ancient glory

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: Moses and the Hebrews (Chapter 9)
readings.challenge: Notice how a historian retells a story that many people read as scripture, and which words show him choosing an explanation.
readings.focus: Van Loon tells the story of the Exodus as the history of a shepherd people and its leader, ending with the claim that the Jews were the first nation to worship one God.
readings.context: The story of Moses comes from the Bible, in the books of Exodus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, which Jews and Christians read as scripture. Van Loon, writing in 1921, retells it as history and adds explanations of his own; historians still debate how much of it can be checked, because few records outside the Bible mention these events. The patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the forefathers of the Hebrews in the book of Genesis; Jehovah is an old English way of writing the Hebrew name of God; peregrinations are wanderings; Ur was a city near the mouth of the Euphrates. Earlier in his book, van Loon tells how King Khufu built the Great Pyramid, which archaeologists date to about 2560 B.C.
readings.contentNote: The chapter describes the Hebrews forced into slavery in Egypt and then taking land from the Canaanites who already lived there. Van Loon tells a sacred story from outside any faith: he calls Jehovah one of many gods of western Asia and leaves open how the words came to be on the tablets, which families may understand differently. He uses the old race label “Semitic.”

excerpt.locator: “Moses,” the whole chapter; opens “Some time during the twentieth century before our era, a small and unimportant tribe of…”; closes “…new home but he had also made the Jews the first of all nations to worship a single God.”.

questions.prompt: What happened to the Hebrews in Egypt after the Hyksos were driven out? Van Loon says they were forced to work “on the Pyramids”: check that against his own dates and the date in the context.
facilitatorNotes: They were made “common slaves,” forced to build royal roads, and kept in by soldiers on the frontiers. But van Loon dates their first wandering to the twentieth century before our era, and the Great Pyramid was already some five hundred years old by then. Unless he means other, later pyramids, the detail does not fit; it reads like a picture added for effect. The Bible itself names store-cities, not pyramids.
evidence: they had been degraded to the rank of common slaves
forced to work on the royal roads and on the Pyramids
Some time during the twentieth century before our era

questions.prompt: Why did Moses want to bring his people back to “the ways of the patriarchs”? What does van Loon think the desert taught him?
facilitatorNotes: In the desert Moses learned the “simple virtues” of ancestors who stayed away from cities and would not be “corrupted by the ease and the luxury” of a foreign civilisation. Van Loon treats the desert as a teacher and the city as a danger. Readers may question this: later in the book he praises Greek cities as the place where freedom grew.
evidence: had refused to let themselves be corrupted by the ease and the luxury of a foreign civilisation
Moses decided to bring his people back to a love of the ways of the patriarchs.

questions.prompt: Read the paragraph about the stone tablets again. What does van Loon say happened, and what does he leave unsaid?
facilitatorNotes: He reports a rumour (“It was whispered”), a storm that hid the mountain, and tablets that came back engraved with “the words which Jehovah had spoken.” He never says who carved them; he tells what the people came to believe. Some readers will take this as a miracle told plainly, others as a historian hinting at a natural explanation; the wording allows both, and families’ own beliefs will shape the reading.
evidence: It was whispered that he had gone away carrying two tablets of rough-hewn stone.
there stood engraved upon the tablets the words which Jehovah had spoken unto the people of Israel

questions.prompt: The new land “seemed pleasant and prosperous,” but “Unfortunately” it was already inhabited. What happened to the people who lived there, and what does “Unfortunately” show about whose side the chapter tells?
facilitatorNotes: The Canaanites were there first, and “the Jews forced their way into the valleys.” “Unfortunately” is unfortunate from the newcomers’ point of view; the Canaanites’ side is not told at all. Readers can retell one sentence as a Canaanite might have told it, and notice how much a single word decides whose story it is.
evidence: Unfortunately, the mainland, Palestine, was already inhabited by another Semitic race, called the Canaanites.
But the Jews forced their way into the valleys

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the alphabet and the Persians (Chapters 10 and 11)
readings.challenge: Separate what van Loon reports from what he judges, especially when he describes a whole people at once.
readings.focus: Traders give the world a quick, simple alphabet; then a new people from the hills builds an empire, and van Loon frames its war with Greece as Asia against Europe.
readings.context: Van Loon has followed the Hebrews to Palestine; the Phoenicians were their neighbours on the coast, in what is now Lebanon. Tyre and Sidon were their chief cities; the Scilly islands lie off the south-western tip of England, near the tin mines of Cornwall; Cadiz is in Spain and Marseilles in France. A monopoly is control of a whole trade by one group; pothooks are scrawled marks. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; today “Indo-European” names a family of related languages, from Hindi and Persian to Greek, Latin and English, not a race of people. “Aryan” was a name some ancient peoples of Iran and India used for themselves; in the twentieth century the idea of an “Aryan race” was used by the Nazis to justify persecuting and murdering Jews and others. Zarathustra (Zoroaster) was a religious teacher of ancient Persia, not the leader of a migration, and Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire around 550 B.C.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon judges the whole Phoenician people as dishonest and friendless on the word of their neighbours, and sorts peoples into races (“Semitic,” “Indo-European,” “Aryan”), calling the old peoples “old and tired” and the newcomers “more energetic”; these are prejudices of his time, not findings. He calls the early Europeans “wild barbarians,” and the chapters describe conquest and war.

excerpt.locator: “The Phœnicians” and “The Indo-Europeans,” both whole chapters; opens “The Phœnicians, who were the neighbours of the Jews, were a Semitic tribe which at a very…”; closes “…will tell you how the struggle between east and west has continued until this very day.”.

questions.prompt: What did the Phoenicians change when they made their alphabet, and what did they give up to do it?
facilitatorNotes: They turned thousands of signs into twenty-two letters, borrowing a few Egyptian pictures and simplifying Sumerian wedges. They gave up “pretty looks” for speed, because busy traders could not spend hours carving a few letters. Readers can compare writing a word in letters with drawing it in pictures.
evidence: They sacrificed the pretty looks of the older system for the advantage of speed
a short and handy alphabet of twenty-two letters

questions.prompt: Van Loon says the Phoenicians “were very unpleasant people and did not have a single friend.” Where does his information come from, and should we trust it?
facilitatorNotes: From their neighbours (“If we are to believe all their neighbours”), who were often their rivals in trade and war, so their opinion is a poor witness. His own facts point another way: trading posts all round the Mediterranean that became cities such as Cadiz and Marseilles, and an alphabet that everyone adopted. Judging a whole people by rivals’ gossip is unfair; readers can say what evidence would be fairer.
evidence: If we are to believe all their neighbours
Indeed they were very unpleasant people and did not have a single friend.
Many of these were the origin of modern cities, such as Cadiz and Marseilles.

questions.prompt: Follow the alphabet from Tyre to the page you are reading. Who changed it at each step?
facilitatorNotes: Phoenicians to Greeks, who “added a few letters of their own”; Greeks to Romans, who “modified the figures”; Romans to the peoples of western Europe; and so to English. The book itself is the proof van Loon points to: it is printed in letters “of Phœnician origin.” Readers can look at A, which began as a picture of an ox’s head.
evidence: The Greeks added a few letters of their own
this book is written in characters that are of Phœnician origin

questions.prompt: Van Loon says the old peoples of the Fertile Valley were “getting old and tired” and the newcomers were “more energetic.” Can a whole people be old or tired? What else might explain why one empire defeats others?
facilitatorNotes: A people is not a person; the words are a metaphor that hides real causes, such as an able leader (Cyrus), better horses or organisation, and quarrels among the old kingdoms. The same habit makes “Asia, the ancient teacher,” and “Europe, the young and eager pupil.” Ask readers whether that tidy picture is a fact or a way of telling the story that puts Europe in the hero’s place.
evidence: the venerable races of the Fertile Valley were getting old and tired
a new and more energetic race appeared upon the horizon
Asia, the ancient teacher, and Europe, the young and eager pupil

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: Troy, Mycenae and Cnossus (Chapter 12)
readings.challenge: Follow how a discovery changes what people believed, and notice where van Loon says he cannot tell.
readings.focus: Digging for a legend, Schliemann found an older civilisation; its ruins tell part of its story and leave the rest unknown.
readings.context: Homer’s Iliad, an ancient Greek poem, tells of the Greeks’ war against Troy and its king, Priam (Priamus in Latin). Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890), a German businessman, began digging at a mound in north-western Turkey (Asia Minor) in 1871, and later at Mycenae in Greece. Mecklenburg is a region of northern Germany; a parson is a minister; the Titans were giants of Greek myth. Schliemann told the story of his boyhood dream himself, years later, and historians now doubt parts of it. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; the people of Crete are now called Minoans. Their own script, Linear A, is still unread, but a later one, Linear B, was deciphered in 1952 and turned out to be an early form of Greek, written by mainland Greeks (the Mycenaeans) who had taken over Cnossus, now spelled Knossos. Why the palace fell is still debated.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon calls the Greeks who conquered the Aegean world “savages” and “a less civilised race,” ranking peoples by how civilised he judges them.

excerpt.locator: “The Ægean Sea,” the whole chapter; opens “When Heinrich Schliemann was a little boy his father told him the story of Troy. He liked…”; closes “…peninsula between the Adriatic and the Ægean seas and who are known to us as Greeks.”.

questions.prompt: What did Schliemann set out to find, and what did his trench actually reach? Why was that a surprise?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted Homer’s Troy, but he dug so fast that his trench went straight through it to a town a thousand years older. Instead of crude stone tools he found statuettes, jewelry and painted vases, so the people before the Greeks had been far more skilled than anyone thought. Van Loon’s dry “enthusiasm was somewhat greater than his knowledge” hints that haste damaged the very layer he wanted.
evidence: his trench went straight through the heart of the city for which he was looking
beautiful statuettes and very costly jewelry
whose enthusiasm was somewhat greater than his knowledge

questions.prompt: Careful study “has done away with some of the romantic features of the story.” Which features, and what replaced them?
facilitatorNotes: The Greeks thought the huge walls were the work of Titans, and the builders seemed like sorcerers; study showed “simple sailors and traders.” The labyrinth of legend becomes a palace with vast storage cellars. Evidence replaces myth with an explanation. Readers may decide whether the true story is less exciting or more.
evidence: were no sorcerers, but simple sailors and traders
had given rise to the story of the “labyrinth,”

questions.prompt: Why does van Loon call Cnossus “entirely modern”? Which details make his case, and is “modern” a good test of a civilisation?
facilitatorNotes: Drains, stoves, winding staircases, a banqueting hall, and the first daily use of the bathtub. He measures the past by the comforts of his own time; a reader could also judge by art, laws, trade or fairness. Ask which test readers would choose and why.
evidence: entirely modern in its insistence upon hygiene and comfort
the first people to make a daily use of the hitherto unknown bathtub

questions.prompt: “That I can not tell.” Find the places where van Loon admits the limits of what is known. Why can’t he tell, and how do historians work without written records?
facilitatorNotes: The Cretan writing could not be read, so the history had to be rebuilt from ruins; “Unless we are very much mistaken” marks his guess about who destroyed it. Ruins can show wealth, fire and sudden change, but not names or reasons. Since 1921 one Cretan script has been read (see the context), which shows how later evidence can change a history.
evidence: what caused its sudden downfall, that I can not tell
no one has yet been able to decipher their inscriptions
Unless we are very much mistaken

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: the Hellenes take Greece (Chapter 13)
readings.challenge: Read a short chapter closely and test its praise and blame against the deeds it describes.
readings.focus: Wandering shepherds conquer the Greek peninsula, learn from the people they find there, and then turn on their teachers.
readings.context: Van Loon has described the rich island civilisation of Crete and the Aegean, which fell to invaders from the north. In Greek myth, Deucalion and Pyrrha survived a great flood sent by Zeus, the chief god, who lived on Mount Olympus. Thucydides (about 460–400 B.C.) wrote the history of the war between Athens and Sparta. The Pelasgians were, in Greek tradition, the people who lived in Greece before the Greeks; the Achaeans are the Greeks of Homer’s poems; Thessaly and the Peloponnesus are regions of Greece; Mycenae and Tiryns were hill-fortresses. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; many historians think Greek-speaking peoples entered Greece gradually around 2000 B.C.; the Aegean peoples’ weapons were bronze, since iron came into wide use only after about 1200 B.C.; and mainland Greeks took over Cnossus around 1450 B.C.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon tells how the Hellenes killed the people already living in Greece, took their farms and cattle, enslaved their wives and daughters, and threw the bodies of enemies to their dogs.

excerpt.locator: “The Greeks,” the whole chapter; opens “The Pyramids were a thousand years old and were beginning to show the first signs of…”; closes “…destroyed in the eleventh century B.C. European history was to begin in all seriousness.”.

questions.prompt: Where does van Loon get his picture of the early Hellenes? What does he admit just before he paints it?
facilitatorNotes: “Of these early Hellenes we know nothing.” He leans on Thucydides, who lived many centuries later and said his ancestors “did not amount to very much,” and on the Greeks’ own songs. Yet he adds vivid details, such as living “like pigs.” Ask how he can be so sure of details after admitting that nothing is known.
evidence: Of these early Hellenes we know nothing.
did not amount to very much
They lived like pigs

questions.prompt: List what the Hellenes did to the Pelasgians. Who made songs about these deeds, and what did the songs praise?
facilitatorNotes: They killed them, stole their farms and cattle, and enslaved their wives and daughters. The conquerors made the songs, praising the courage of their own Achaean leaders. Winners often tell the story of a war; readers can ask what a Pelasgian song would have said.
evidence: made their wives and daughters slaves
wrote endless songs praising the courage of the clan of the Achæans

questions.prompt: Why did the Hellenes leave the Aegean castles alone at first, and what did they do instead?
facilitatorNotes: They feared the Aegeans’ metal swords and spears, having only stone axes. Instead they visited, learned to handle metal weapons, to sail and to build boats: “He was a clever pupil.” Curiosity and learning come before conquest.
evidence: they feared the metal swords and the spears of the Ægean soldiers
He was a clever pupil.

questions.prompt: When the pupil had learned everything, he “turned upon his teachers.” Van Loon calls this time “the beginning of Greek civilisation.” Is it fair to start a great civilisation’s story with the destruction of another?
facilitatorNotes: He admires what the Greeks became and still tells plainly how it began: in conquest, theft and slavery. “Civilisation” here means cities, ships and learning, not kindness. Some readers will say learning from others and then surpassing them is how many peoples have risen; others will say the Aegean civilisation, already there, deserves to be called a beginning too.
evidence: he turned upon his teachers and drove them back to their islands
That moment was the beginning of Greek civilisation.
European history was to begin in all seriousness.

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: little cities that were states (Chapter 14)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument from cause to effect, and decide whether the evidence supports each step.
readings.focus: Van Loon argues that small cities, where everyone knew everyone, taught the Greeks moderation and drove them to perfection.
readings.context: Van Loon has told how wandering Greek tribes settled the peninsula and learned from the Aegean peoples. Hellas is the Greeks’ own name for Greece; Sparta, Athens and Thebes were Greek cities; the Acropolis is the rocky hill at the centre of Athens; Ur was a city of ancient Mesopotamia; to pay tribute is to pay a ruler because he has conquered you. Van Loon lived in the United States, and his opening teases Americans’ pride in size. Alexander of Macedonia (356–323 B.C.) conquered an empire from Greece to India; after him the new Greek city of Alexandria, in Egypt, became the ancient world’s greatest centre of science and learning, which van Loon does not mention here.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon calls the peoples of Babylon, Assyria and Egypt “a vast mob,” a sweeping judgment of whole nations. His proud Greek “free citizen” is always a man; he does not say here that women, foreigners and enslaved people had no vote.

excerpt.locator: “The Greek Cities,” the whole chapter; opens “We modern people love the sound of the word “big.” We pride ourselves upon the fact that…”; closes “…become part of a big nation, the old Greek spirit died. And it has been dead ever since.”.

questions.prompt: Why was the runner who boasted about standing on one foot driven out of Sparta? What does the story show about the Greeks?
facilitatorNotes: He was proud of a feat “any common goose” could beat: a showy, useless sort of greatness. For van Loon this shows how far the Greek love of moderation and good sense went, even with popular athletes. Readers may find the punishment too harsh, which is itself a question about moderation.
evidence: he could stand longer on one foot than any other man in Hellas
at which he could be beaten by any common goose

questions.prompt: What did a peasant of Ur mean when he said he was a Babylonian, and what did a Greek mean when he said he was an Athenian?
facilitatorNotes: The Babylonian was “one of millions” paying tribute to whatever king ruled at the moment; the Athenian meant a small town that was both his home and his country, ruled by “the will of the people in the market-place.” One belongs to an empire, the other to a community he helps to run.
evidence: he meant that he was one of millions of other people who paid tribute
which recognised no master but the will of the people in the market-place

questions.prompt: “Don’t you see how these surroundings must have influenced a man?” Explain van Loon’s chain of reasons from small city to perfect work. Which link is strongest, and which weakest?
facilitatorNotes: Small town; everyone knows everyone; neighbours watch and judge your work; so you strive for perfection; and perfection needs moderation. “Must have” shows a reasoned guess, not proof. Readers may find the watching neighbours convincing, or argue that being watched can also make people afraid to try anything new.
evidence: He felt that his intelligent neighbours were watching him.
This knowledge forced him to strive after perfection

questions.prompt: “The old Greek spirit died. And it has been dead ever since.” What does van Loon say happened after Alexander’s conquests? Can a claim like this be proved?
facilitatorNotes: Greek talent moved to great royal capitals and lost its joy and moderation; the Greeks “became cheap artisans.” It is a sweeping opinion: what would count as evidence for the death of a “spirit”? The context mentions Alexandria’s scholars, a strong case against him. Notice too how the chapter began, mocking the modern love of “big”: van Loon is arguing about his own country as much as describing Greece.
evidence: They became cheap artisans, content with second-rate work.
And it has been dead ever since.
We modern people love the sound of the word “big.”

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: tyrants, Draco and Solon (Chapter 15)
readings.challenge: Follow a series of changes in government and the reason van Loon gives for each.
readings.focus: Growing inequality brought nobles and tyrants to power; Athens answered with new laws, citizen juries and a duty for every freeman to take part.
readings.context: Van Loon has argued that the Greeks lived in small independent cities where every citizen knew his neighbours; here he tells how Athens came to be governed by its citizens. Nobles were rich landowning families; a tyrant, in Greek, was a ruler who seized power without a lawful right to it, whether he ruled well or badly; a capital offence is a crime punished by death; jurisprudence is the system of law; a grievance is a complaint of unfair treatment; “demos” is Greek for the people, as in “democracy.” In Athens only free men born to citizen families could take part; women, foreigners and enslaved people could not. The book was written in 1921, and some of its science and dates have since been corrected; Draco’s laws date from about 621 B.C., near the end of the seventh century, and Solon’s reforms from about 594 B.C.
readings.contentNote: Draco’s laws punished even small thefts with death, and van Loon jokes about hanging.

excerpt.locator: “Greek Self-Government,” the whole chapter; opens “In the beginning, all the Greeks had been equally rich and equally poor. Every man had…”; closes “…and to rely upon themselves for their salvation and that was a very good thing.”.

questions.prompt: How were decisions made in the early Greek village? What could the villagers do to a war leader once the danger was over?
facilitatorNotes: All the citizens met in the market-place, and an older man made sure “everybody had a chance to express his views.” A war leader chosen by the people could be removed by them afterwards. Power was lent, not owned; the rest of the chapter shows how that was lost and partly won back.
evidence: it was his duty to see that everybody had a chance to express his views
claimed an equal right to deprive him of his job

questions.prompt: Van Loon gives four reasons why some citizens grew rich and others poor. What are they? Has he left any out?
facilitatorNotes: Hard work, laziness, bad luck and dishonesty. Readers may add inheritance, debt, war, or owning more land to begin with. His own next paragraphs show another cause: once rich, nobles could “buy the best weapons” and take “an undue share” of land, so wealth bought power and more wealth. Ask whether “lazy” is a fair explanation of poverty.
evidence: Some people had worked hard and others had been lazy.
had got hold of an undue share of the farms and estates
They were able to buy the best weapons

questions.prompt: Why did Draco’s laws fail, according to van Loon, and how were Solon’s different?
facilitatorNotes: Draco was “out of touch with ordinary life”: his laws were so harsh, with death for stealing an apple, that they could not be carried out. Solon had travelled and studied, and chose moderation: he helped the peasants without ruining the nobles and let a citizen with a grievance take his case to a jury of fellow citizens. Readers can discuss why laws that are too harsh may protect people less, not more.
evidence: There would not have been rope enough to hang all the criminals
He tried to improve the condition of the peasant without however destroying the prosperity of the nobles
a citizen with a grievance had the right to state his case before a jury of thirty of his fellow Athenians

questions.prompt: Under Solon no freeman could stay at home saying “oh, I am too busy today.” Van Loon admits that government by the people was “often far from successful.” Why does he still call it “a very good thing”? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: It taught the Greeks “to be independent and to rely upon themselves.” Its faults were real: “too much idle talk” and spiteful rivalries. Readers may compare it with voting or class councils today, or point out that it left most of the city’s people out (see the context).
evidence: oh, I am too busy today
There was too much idle talk.
that was a very good thing

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: freemen, slaves and simple living (Chapter 16)
readings.challenge: Notice what a writer’s own details reveal that his summary leaves out.
readings.focus: Van Loon praises Greek simplicity and freedom, while his own description shows that the freedom of a few rested on the work of many enslaved people and on women kept at home.
readings.context: Van Loon has told how Athens came to be governed by its free citizens meeting in the market-place. “Barbarians” was the Greeks’ word for all foreigners; Aeschylus and Euripides wrote plays for the Athenian theatre; Zeus was the chief Greek god; omnipotence is unlimited power. Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852), by Harriet Beecher Stowe, was a famous American novel against slavery. Historians today describe Greek slavery as cruel: most enslaved people were captives of war or children of slaves, they could be bought, sold and beaten, and many laboured and died in the silver mines near Athens. Van Loon’s count of five or six slaves to every citizen is probably too high.
readings.contentNote: Van Loon says slavery in Greece was mild, that belonging to a slave-holding city was “very pleasant,” and that the Greeks thought no city could be civilised without slaves; he does not ask what enslaved people thought. He describes married women kept at home as a matter of “good form” and calls bright colours an “Asiatic fashion.”

excerpt.locator: “Greek Life,” the whole chapter; opens “But how, you will ask, did the ancient Greeks have time to look after their families and…”; closes “…and be truly free in spirit, they reduced their daily needs to the lowest possible point.”.

questions.prompt: In the description of a Greek home, count the people marked “(who was a slave).” What work does each do, and what does the master do?
facilitatorNotes: The cook, the children’s teacher, the seamstresses and the farm overseer; earlier, tailors, carpenters, jewelers, teachers and book-keepers. The master inspects accounts and goes to meetings and plays. The repeated brackets make a point the chapter’s praise of “simplicity” skips: the simple life was simple for the master.
evidence: the cook (who was a slave)
the teacher (who was also a slave)
the master was inspecting the accounts

questions.prompt: Van Loon compares Athens to “a modern club” in which “it was very pleasant to be a member.” From whose point of view is that true? How might the same city look to the cook?
facilitatorNotes: To a freeborn citizen, a “hereditary member.” The enslaved were “hereditary servants,” born into it and unable to leave. Readers can describe one day in the courtyard from the cook’s or the teacher’s point of view.
evidence: Indeed, ancient Athens resembled a modern club.
it was very pleasant to be a member of the organisation

questions.prompt: How does van Loon argue that Greek slavery was not so bad? Is his evidence enough?
facilitatorNotes: He compares it with worse cases: American slavery in Uncle Tom’s Cabin, Rome, and poor free farm-hands, and says city slaves were often better off than poor freemen. Showing that something else was worse does not show that this was good; he gives no enslaved person’s own account, and enslaved people could still be sold and could not choose their lives. The context adds what historians know now.
evidence: we do not mean the sort of people about whom you have read
many of the slaves were more prosperous than the poorer classes of the freemen
The Greeks accepted slavery as a necessary institution

questions.prompt: The chapter ends: the Greeks “wanted to be ‘free,’ both in mind and in body.” Using the chapter, explain whose freedom that was and what made it possible. Does his point about “things” making us their slaves still hold?
facilitatorNotes: It was the free men’s freedom, made possible by enslaved workers and by wives who “rarely left her domain.” Taken on its own, his point about possessions is worth discussing: caring for things does eat time. But using “slave” for owning too many chairs sits oddly in a chapter about real slavery. Readers may agree with the lesson and still question the example.
evidence: The Greeks, before everything else, wanted to be “free,”
In the end they invariably make him their slave
who rarely left her domain

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: from goat-singers to tragedy (Chapter 17)
readings.challenge: Follow a step-by-step development and the word histories that explain it, keeping each stage in order.
readings.focus: Van Loon traces drama from a noisy procession for the god of wine to plays the Greeks took as seriously as an election.
readings.context: Van Loon has described the simple daily life of the Greeks. Dionysos (Dionysus) was the Greek god of wine, and Satyrs were his half-goat companions; Attica is the countryside around Athens; pipes of Pan are a row of reed pipes played by blowing across them. The “inventive young poet from the village of Icaria” is known by tradition as Thespis, which is why actors are still called thespians. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote tragedies, and Aristophanes comedies, in Athens in the fifth century B.C.; Hamlet is a tragedy by Shakespeare. When van Loon wrote, alcohol was banned in the United States, and soda fountains, counters selling fizzy drinks and ice cream, were popular meeting places. Scholars still argue about why tragedy was called a “goat song”; van Loon gives one explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Greek Theatre,” the whole chapter; opens “At a very early stage of their history the Greeks had begun to collect the poems, which…”; closes “…honors than those bestowed upon a general who had just returned from a famous victory.”.

questions.prompt: What do the Greek words “tragos” and “oidos” have to do with tragedy? Where does the word “scenery” come from?
facilitatorNotes: Tragos means goat and oidos singer, so a “goat singer” in goat-skins gave his name to tragedy. Skene was the tent where actors put on masks, so the stage’s background is the “scenery.” Word histories carry old customs inside modern words; readers can look for another word whose history surprises them.
evidence: The Greek word for goat is “tragos” and the Greek word for singer is “oidos.”
The Greek word for tent is “skene”

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order: how did a procession become a play, and a play with one actor become a play with many?
facilitatorNotes: A chorus in goat-skins sang in the procession; the crowd grew bored, since the Greeks thought dullness as bad as ugliness or sickness; a poet had one singer step out and talk with the bandmaster, so dialogue and acting began; acting soon mattered more than the parade; Aeschylus used two actors, Sophocles three, Euripides as many as he liked; the chorus shrank to bystanders. Each step answers the audience’s wish for something new.
evidence: He made one of the members of the goat-chorus step forward
introduced two “actors” instead of one
the Greeks thought dullness an evil only comparable to ugliness or sickness

questions.prompt: Van Loon compares Dionysos to “a God of the Soda-Fountain” and the Greek orchestra to seats costing “three dollars and thirty cents.” Why does he keep bringing in American life of 1921? Do the comparisons still work?
facilitatorNotes: They make the far past familiar and funny for his first readers. But jokes about everyday things age fast: a reader today needs the context to know that alcohol was then banned and soda fountains were popular. Readers can invent a comparison of their own for a modern reader, and predict how long it would last.
evidence: as popular as a God of the Soda-Fountain would be in our own land
where you pay three dollars and thirty cents for a seat

questions.prompt: A successful playwright was received “with greater honors” than a victorious general. Why might a city honour a playwright so highly? Would that happen today?
facilitatorNotes: The Greeks “never went to the theatre to give their minds a vacation”; plays were part of religious festivals and civic life, as important as an election, and asked serious questions about gods and wrongdoing. Readers may compare how we honour writers, film-makers, athletes and soldiers, and say what that shows about what a society values.
evidence: never went to the theatre to give their minds a vacation
a successful playwright was received with greater honors than those bestowed upon a general

readings.title: The Story of Mankind: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis (Chapter 18)
readings.challenge: Keep three Persian invasions and their battles in order, and notice where legend and the gods enter a history.
readings.focus: Van Loon tells the Persian Wars as Europe defending itself against Asia, with heroes, a traitor, a storm sent by a god and a city that could not stay united.
readings.context: Van Loon has described the Greek cities and their ways of life; now the Persian Empire, which ruled from Egypt to India, turns on Greece. King Darius sent forces in 492 and 490 B.C., and his son Xerxes in 480–479 B.C. Lydia was a kingdom in what is now western Turkey, where many Greek colonies stood; Mount Athos is a mountain on a peninsula of northern Greece; the Piraeus is the port of Athens; an isthmus is a narrow neck of land; a garrison is a group of soldiers guarding a place. Most of what we know comes from the Greek historian Herodotus, writing a generation later. The story of a runner who carried the news of Marathon to Athens and then died appears only in writers who lived centuries afterward, though the marathon race is named after it, and van Loon’s army sizes are far too large.
readings.contentNote: Battle and death run through the chapter: Persian messengers are thrown into a well, a fleet drowns, a runner dies after bringing news, and Leonidas and his soldiers are killed. Van Loon calls the Persians “hordes” and tells the war as Europe against Asia, a way of speaking common in his time that takes the Greek side.

excerpt.locator: “The Persian Wars,” the whole chapter; opens “The Greeks had learned the art of trading from the Ægeans who had been the pupils of the…”; closes “…the hour of victory and enthusiasm to slip by, and the same opportunity never returned.”.

questions.prompt: According to the opening paragraphs, what started the quarrel between Persia and the Greeks? Find at least two causes.
facilitatorNotes: The Persians demanded a yearly tax from the Greek colonies on the coast of Asia Minor, the colonies refused and called on Greece for help; the Persian kings saw free Greek cities as “bad examples” to their subjects; and the Phoenicians, losing trade to the Greeks, offered Persia their ships. Readers can rank the causes and say which van Loon seems to think most important.
evidence: The Greek colonies objected. The Persians insisted.
very dangerous political institutions and bad examples

questions.prompt: Where in this chapter do the gods, or a legend, enter the history? How should a reader treat those parts?
facilitatorNotes: The “Storm-God” blowing out his cheeks to wreck the fleet near Mount Athos: the storm was real, the god is the Greeks’ explanation, told in their voice. Pheidippides whispering “We have won” and dying is a later legend (see the context). Readers can rewrite the storm sentence as a plain weather report and compare the two.
evidence: the Storm-God blew his cheeks until he almost burst the veins of his brow
“We have won,” he whispered and then he died

questions.prompt: What did Sparta do well and what did it do badly in these wars? Why do you think van Loon calls the defeat at Thermopylae a “victory”?
facilitatorNotes: Badly: it refused help before Marathon out of envy and neglected to guard the passes. Well: Leonidas held the pass “with unequalled bravery,” and at Plataea the Spartans at last “understood the seriousness of the hour.” Thermopylae was lost, but the stand earned honour and time, so van Loon counts it a victory of courage. Readers may disagree: a lost pass let the Persians burn Athens.
evidence: But Sparta was envious of the fame of Athens
He fought and held the pass with unequalled bravery.
But this time the Spartans understood the seriousness of the hour.
In this way the victory of Thermopylae came to naught.

questions.prompt: The Persians are “too civilised to plunder,” yet also “hordes” and “disorganised Asiatic troops.” What do van Loon’s word choices show about whose side he takes? Is the war really “Asia” against “Europe”?
facilitatorNotes: The Greeks get names and heroes; the Persians are a faceless crowd, though he admits they ruled their subjects without plunder. His own story weakens the Asia-against-Europe picture: Phoenicians help Persia, and Greek cities refuse to help each other. Ask readers how a Persian historian might have told the same years.
evidence: The Persians were too civilised to plunder their new subjects.
against the hordes of the Persians
Asia made ready to destroy the rising power of Europe
